solution:
The proposed process is \({}^{56}_{26}\text{Fe} \to 2\,{}^{28}_{13}\text{Al}\). The parent atom carries 26 electrons and the two fragment atoms carry \(2 \times 13 = 26\) between them, so the electron masses cancel exactly and the atomic masses given may be used directly in \(Q\).

Mass difference:

\(\Delta m = m({}^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}) - 2\,m({}^{28}_{13}\text{Al}) = 55.93494\,\text{u} - 2(27.98191\,\text{u})\)

\(\Delta m = 55.93494\,\text{u} - 55.96382\,\text{u} = -0.02888\,\text{u}\)

Using \(1\,\text{u} = 931.5\,\text{MeV}/c^2\),

\(Q = (\Delta m)c^2 = (-0.02888)(931.5)\,\text{MeV} = -26.9\,\text{MeV}\)

The products are heavier than the parent, so \(Q\) is negative: energy would have to be supplied from outside rather than released. The process is endothermic and therefore not energetically possible on its own. This is what the binding-energy curve requires: \({}^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}\) sits at the peak of the binding energy per nucleon, so any splitting of it moves the nucleons to a less tightly bound state and must cost energy.

\(Q = -26.9\,\text{MeV}\); the fission is not energetically possible (endothermic).

Find the number of \({}^{239}_{94}\text{Pu}\) atoms in the sample, then multiply by the energy per fission.

Converting the mass, \(1\,\text{kg} = 1000\,\text{g}\), and the molar mass of \({}^{239}_{94}\text{Pu}\) is \(239\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), so the amount of substance is

\(n = \dfrac{1000\,\text{g}}{239\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 4.184\,\text{mol}\)

Number of atoms, with \(N_A = 6.023 \times 10^{23}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\):

\(N = n N_A = (4.184)(6.023 \times 10^{23}) = 2.52 \times 10^{24}\)

Every atom undergoes fission and each fission releases \(180\,\text{MeV}\), so

\(E = N \times 180\,\text{MeV} = (2.52 \times 10^{24})(180) = 4.54 \times 10^{26}\,\text{MeV}\)

For comparison, with \(1\,\text{MeV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-13}\,\text{J}\) this is \(E = (4.54 \times 10^{26})(1.6 \times 10^{-13}) = 7.26 \times 10^{13}\,\text{J}\).

\(E = 4.54 \times 10^{26}\,\text{MeV}\) (equivalently \(7.26 \times 10^{13}\,\text{J}\)).

Count the deuterons, halve that to get the number of fusion events (the reaction consumes two deuterons each time), convert the released energy to joules and divide by the power.

Converting the mass, \(2.0\,\text{kg} = 2000\,\text{g}\), and taking the molar mass of \({}^{2}_{1}\text{H}\) as \(2.0\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\),

\(N = \dfrac{2000\,\text{g}}{2.0\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} \times 6.023 \times 10^{23}\,\text{mol}^{-1} = 6.023 \times 10^{26}\) deuterons

Each event uses two deuterons, so the number of fusion events is

\(N_{\text{f}} = \dfrac{N}{2} = 3.01 \times 10^{26}\)

Energy released, at \(3.27\,\text{MeV}\) per event:

\(E = (3.01 \times 10^{26})(3.27\,\text{MeV}) = 9.85 \times 10^{26}\,\text{MeV}\)

Converting with \(1\,\text{MeV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-13}\,\text{J}\):

\(E = (9.85 \times 10^{26})(1.6 \times 10^{-13}\,\text{J}) = 1.58 \times 10^{14}\,\text{J}\)

The lamp consumes \(P = 100\,\text{W} = 100\,\text{J s}^{-1}\), so

\(t = \dfrac{E}{P} = \dfrac{1.58 \times 10^{14}\,\text{J}}{100\,\text{J s}^{-1}} = 1.58 \times 10^{12}\,\text{s}\)

With \(1\,\text{year} = 3.154 \times 10^{7}\,\text{s}\),

\(t = \dfrac{1.58 \times 10^{12}}{3.154 \times 10^{7}} = 5.0 \times 10^{4}\,\text{years}\)

\(t = 1.58 \times 10^{12}\,\text{s} \approx 5.0 \times 10^{4}\,\text{years}\).

Treating each deuteron as a hard sphere of radius \(r = 2.0\,\text{fm}\), the two just touch when their centres are separated by

\(d = 2r = 2(2.0\,\text{fm}) = 4.0\,\text{fm} = 4.0 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{m}\)

A deuteron has one proton, so each carries charge \(q = e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\). The height of the barrier is the electrostatic potential energy of the pair at that separation:

\(U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\dfrac{e^2}{d} = \dfrac{(9 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-2})(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C})^2}{4.0 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{m}}\)

\(U = \dfrac{(9 \times 10^{9})(2.56 \times 10^{-38})}{4.0 \times 10^{-15}}\,\text{J} = 5.76 \times 10^{-14}\,\text{J}\)

Converting with \(1\,\text{MeV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-13}\,\text{J}\):

\(U = \dfrac{5.76 \times 10^{-14}\,\text{J}}{1.6 \times 10^{-13}\,\text{J MeV}^{-1}} = 0.36\,\text{MeV}\)

So the two deuterons must between them bring \(0.36\,\text{MeV}\) of kinetic energy to the collision; if they approach with equal speeds each needs about \(0.18\,\text{MeV}\).

Height of the potential barrier \(U = 5.76 \times 10^{-14}\,\text{J} = 0.36\,\text{MeV} = 360\,\text{keV}\).
